doc.title: Bobby Gordon interviewed by Monk Rowe, Chautauqua, New York, September 12, 1997

title: What goes on in his head when improvising
summary: Gordon plays the melody first, then improvises on chord changes he keeps in his head, using borrowed licks from Russell and Marsala.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Well here’s a hard question. When you’re improvising, can you describe to me what’s going on in your head?

Well if you’re playing a tune, say like “Rosetta” or something like that, written by Earl Hines and Walter Thor, I play the melody if I’m playing by myself, I play the melody the first chorus. I try to remember the melody, I try to play the melody most of the time on the first chorus. And then I would change into a jazz chorus and I would think ahead of time in my head, which chord progressions are coming up next. I know F is coming here and D7 is coming there and G7 is coming there — I have it all stored in my head I hope. And I improvise on those chord changes on the song. That’s how I do it.
Do you think that there are Bobby Gordon licks?
I wouldn’t say there are any Bobby Gordon licks, no. Stolen licks from Pee Wee Russell and Joe Marsala maybe.
And then you try to make them your own, right?
